title: Lung Adenocarcinoma With Initially Co‐Occurring EGFR and BRAF Double Mutation: A Case Report and Literature Review
author: Lu Wang; Xueting Wang; Motong Xu; Yanan Wang; Lingxin Feng; Xue Yang; Jing Wang
text:
ABSTRACT
Vrafmurine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B (BRAF) mutations, including both V600E and non‐V600E variants, are infrequent in non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), representing approximately 2% of lung adenocarcinomas. Activated BRAF mutations are regarded as an underappreciated oncogenic driver in NSCLC, typically occurring in a mutually exclusive manner with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations, as well as ALK and ROS1 rearrangements. In recent years, advancements in multiple‐gene panel testing have demonstrated that EGFR mutations and BRAF mutations can coexist. Notably, the secondary BRAF V600E mutation has been identified as one of the mechanisms contributing to resistance against EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in EGFR‐mutated lung adenocarcinomas. However, the role of co‐occurring BRAF mutations and associated treatment strategies in patients with EGFR mutations has not been thoroughly investigated. Additionally, the profile of adverse events related to combination therapy has not been previously evaluated. This case report presents a patient with co‐occurring EGFR and BRAF mutations who demonstrated a sustained response and tolerance to adverse events when treated with a combination of Osimertinib, Trametinib, and Dabrafenib.
Keywords: BRAF, co‐mutation, EGFR, NSCLC

1. Introduction
Activating mutations of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) in non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) serve as a favorable predictive biomarker for treatment with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). The most prevalent activating mutations include in‐frame deletions in exon 19 and a single‐point mutation at exon 21 (Leu858Arg), which collectively account for over 80% of identified activating EGFR mutations. In contrast, BRAF represents a rare mutation site, exhibiting a mutation rate of only 2% in NSCLC. This gene encodes members of the RAF family of threonine/serine protein kinases, which function as extracellular signals to activate RAS–RAF–MEK regulated kinases, thereby playing a crucial role in the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway [1]. In lung cancer, BRAF mutations typically function as oncogenic driver genes in NSCLC and are generally mutually exclusive with EGFR mutations, as well as ALK and ROS1 rearrangements. Secondary BRAF mutations have been observed in instances of drug resistance following treatment with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). However, cases of primary double mutations involving both EGFR and BRAF are rare, and there is a notable lack of research regarding therapeutic strategies for such conditions. Furthermore, there are currently no FDA‐approved treatment options available for these patients. This case report presents the identification of both EGFR and BRAF mutations in the tumor tissue of a male smoker diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. The patient demonstrated a prolonged response to the combination therapy consisting of Osimertinib, Dabrafenib, and Trametinib, without experiencing intolerable adverse effects.
1.1. Case Presentation
In April 2023, a 65‐year‐old male patient presented to our hospital with a complaint of sputum production. The symptoms had persisted for 1 month and were not accompanied by chest tightness or pain. The patient has a smoking history exceeding 20 years and reports no family history of genetic disorders. Physical examination revealed a palpable mass in the right chest wall, measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter, characterized by its firmness and indistinct borders relative to the surrounding tissue. Additionally, an enlarged lymph node was palpated in the right axilla, also measuring around 2.5 cm in diameter. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest demonstrated a mass located within the right chest wall as well as irregular nodules present in the upper lobe of the right lung. Subsequently, positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) revealed positive lesions in the right chest wall, the upper lobe of the right lung, and several lymph nodes in the mediastinum, axillae, and supraclavicular region (Figure 1). The standard uptake value for these sites was above 2.5. A puncture biopsy of the right chest wall mass and the right axillary lymph nodes was performed on April 24, 2023, and the pathologic results suggested that the tumor of the right chest wall originated from the lung. A CT‐guided needle lung puncture biopsy of the upper lobe of the right lung was conducted on April 27, 2023, with the pathology showing moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma (Figure 2). Furthermore, genetic testing for common lung cancers using next‐generation sequencing (NGS) revealed a double mutation of EGFR‐19 del and BRAF V600E (Figure 3).
In accordance with the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC)/Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) 8th edition Tumor Node Metastasis (TNM) staging classification, the patient was initially diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma (CT2aN3M1b IVA), chest wall metastasis, and lymph node metastasis in the mediastinum, axillae, and supraclavicular regions. Referring to the 2023 Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) guidelines and National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines, targeted therapy is preferred for stage IV non‐small cell lung cancer with EGFR or BRAF mutations. Considering that the patient in this case had a primary EGFR and BRAF double mutation, we tried to select a multi‐drug combination therapy. The treatment plan was formulated as follows: (1) oral targeted drug Osimertinib mesylate 80 mg once daily (qd); (2) oral Trametinib 2 mg once daily (qd); (3) oral Dabrafenib mesylate 250 mg twice daily (bid). The patient was treated with Osimertinib in combination with Trametinib and Dabrafenib from May 18, 2023, and follow‐up every 2 months to assess efficacy.
The follow‐up CT reexamination conducted on June 15, 2023, indicated a total reduction in target lesion diameters of 30.9%. The efficacy was evaluated as partial remission (PR) according to RESIST 1.1 guidelines. At subsequent follow‐ups, the efficacy of the treatment was sustained in PR. During the course of treatment, the patient experienced low fever, intermittent diarrhea, and grade I‐II liver function abnormality, which improved after symptomatic treatment. Due to the patient's persistent low‐grade fever, the dose of dabrafenib was reduced to 75 mg qd. By the time of the follow‐up in June 2024, the patient's PFS had already been more than 13 months, and the treatment did not show any serious adverse reactions.
2. Discussion
In non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), EGFR is a classic mutation with a mutation rate of about 50% in the Asian population. EGFR mutations are more prevalent among women, non‐smokers, and individuals with adenocarcinoma. Furthermore, the survival rate of patients harboring EGFR mutations is higher compared with that of patients with wild‐type EGFR [2]. With the advent of the first‐, second‐, and third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs, the survival of these patients has been significantly extended, and the response rate can reach as high as 80% [3]. Furthermore, research has demonstrated that patients with complex mutations exhibit the same sensitivity to EGFR TKI treatment as those with classic mutations. In cases involving rare exon mutations, EGFR‐TKI should also be considered as both first‐line and second‐line therapy [4]. However, most patients develop acquired resistance within 8–14 months after initiating treatment. Therefore, treating NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations remains a major challenge. Compared with EGFR mutations, BRAF mutations have a lower mutation rate, accounting for about 1%–3% of NSCLCs, of which approximately 50% are BRAF V600E mutations. Tumors with BRAF V600E mutations are generally more aggressive histologically, and their high heterogeneity is inversely correlated with treatment efficacy [5]. The BRAF inhibitor trametinib combined with the MEK inhibitor dabrafenib as first‐ and second‐line treatment for advanced NSCLC had an overall response rate of 64% and 63.2%, respectively, the study showed. Guidelines from the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO), and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) recommend BRAF inhibitors in combination with MEK inhibitors as first‐line treatment for patients with advanced BRAF‐mutated NSCLC [6, 7].
In lung adenocarcinomas, mutations in driver genes such as EGFR, BRAF, etc., are often considered mutually exclusive; however, cases of lung adenocarcinomas with EGFR mutations and secondary BRAF V600E mutations have been shown to be one of the mechanisms leading to acquired resistance to EGFR‐TKI [8]. By analyzing the follow‐up treatment of 35 patients with secondary BRAF mutations after EGFR‐TKI treatment, Professor Zhou's team found that the PFS of the chemotherapy group, the TKIs group that received no EGFR and BRAF mutations, and the group that received the combination of EGFR and BRAF inhibitors was 5.0, 2.1, and 7.8 months, respectively [9]. These results suggest that such patients are more likely to benefit from the combination of targeted drugs against both EGFR and BRAF.
In lung adenocarcinomas with both EGFR and BRAF mutations, most BRAF mutations are secondary, and primary double mutations are very rare. However, the occurrence of primary EGFR and BRAF mutations in lung adenocarcinoma has been reported recently, which may be associated with tumor heterogeneity. Moreover, the effectiveness of single‐target drugs is not high in patients with co‐mutations. Haiyan Zhang et al. detected BRAF V600E and EGFR gene mutations using second‐generation high‐throughput sequencing on pathological specimens from 225 NSCLC patients at Hubei Cancer Hospital. A total of four cases with primary double mutations were identified, with one patient untreated, two patients receiving gefitinib and showing PFS of 4 and 7 months, respectively, and one patient treated with osimertinib, with a PFS of 5 months [10]. Morikawa et al. reported a case of lung adenocarcinoma with bone metastasis, where double mutations of EGFR L858R and BRAF V600E were detected in both the primary and metastatic lesions. The patient's PFS after treatment with afatinib was only 12 days, with a clear benefit after switching to trametinib and dabrafenib, and the efficacy evaluation was PR [11]. The specific PFS time was not clearly reported. However, in the aforementioned cases, only targeted drugs targeting a single gene were selected, and the PFS durations were short. This may be due to the continuous activation of downstream non‐EGFR signals caused by the BRAF mutation. Therefore, EGFR‐TKI alone could not completely inhibit the activation of downstream tumor‐related signaling pathways. In the present case, we report a patient with co‐mutations of EGFR and BRAF, with mutation abundances of 10.33% and 3.51%, respectively. Considering the low abundance of both target mutations and the poor efficacy of single‐target agents in this case, we selected a combination of three agents as first‐line therapy, resulting in a PFS of over 13 months with ongoing follow‐up. To our knowledge, this is the first case where a three‐drug combination has achieved the longest progression‐free survival (Figure 4).
In patients with driver co‐mutations, clinicians may opt to target a single drug as the combination could exacerbate the occurrence of adverse reactions. The patient in this case also experienced grade 1–2 adverse events, including fever, diarrhea, and abnormal liver function; all of these were resolved with symptomatic treatment. This suggests that combination therapy may be feasible for patients with primary co‐mutations of EGFR and BRAF.
In summary, EGFR‐BRAF primary co‐mutated NSCLC cases are rare, and there is currently no guidance‐based evidence for single‐target or combination therapy. We are the first to report the use of osimertinib in combination with trametinib and dabrafenib as first‐line therapy, which yields the longest PFS benefit without an increase in associated adverse effects. However, the mechanism of the EGFR and BRAF double mutation, as well as drug efficacy and adverse effects, needs to be verified in the future with data from a larger sample size.
